paper.title: JudgeFlow: Agentic Workflow Optimization via Block Judge
paper.central_claim: A block-level Judge that ranks logic blocks by responsibility for failed runs lets an LLM optimizer focus edits on the most problematic block, improving sample efficiency and final performance of automatically optimized agentic workflows on math reasoning and code generation benchmarks versus existing methods.

signatures.object: Code-represented agentic workflow decomposed into <=3 logic blocks (seq/for/cond) of configured LLM operators (operator prompts, backbone, parameters)
signatures.information: Judge sees problem, ground-truth answer, wrong answer, execution trace and per-block I/O of failed runs (threshold eps=1); optimizer sees selected block, workflow, action set, few-shot failure logs for that block, and banned prior workflows
signatures.operation: Evaluate W on data D; for each failure a Judge LLM ranks blocks by responsibility; min-sum of ranks across failures picks B_sel; optimizer LLM applies one of Add/Remove/Modify to B_sel
signatures.conditions: Tasks with ground-truth answers and executable evaluator (GSM8K, MATH, AIME, MBPP, HumanEval)
signatures.feedback: Pass/fail score plus LLM Judge blame
signatures.selection_rule_data: W' scored and inserted in top-K=3 pool; start workflow softmax-sampled from pool; selection on the training split
signatures.persistence: Workflow code/config in the candidate pool across 20 rounds; best workflow deployed
signatures.later_use: Next round's parent workflow and 'previous optimization' ban list
signatures.claimed_effect: Avg 82.2 vs 80.8 best baseline; faster early gains than AFlow on MBPP
signatures.failure_boundary: Judge reliability untested; <=3-block space; no cross-model transfer; one tie to AFlow-style infrastructure

signatures.object: Reused operator library and fixed optimizer (not itself edited)
signatures.operation: Improver is held fixed; only the task workflow changes
signatures.failure_boundary: Improver-level evidence level cannot be reached

gap.author_gap: Workflow optimizers rely on coarse end-to-end evaluation signals and lack fine-grained signals on where to refine, giving inefficient or low-impact modifications; MCTS expansion/evaluation is expensive.
gap.checked_gap: Real limitation cited from AFlow-style MCTS search and from failure-attribution work (Zhang et al. 2025c); the paper provides no measurement of how often coarse-signal search wastes evaluations beyond one AFlow curve.
gap.lineage_closest_adjacent: AFlow (MCTS over operator code, Zhang 2025b), MaAS, MermaidFlow, ADAS, GPTSwarm; prompt-level textual gradients (TextGrad, Pryzant 2023); automated failure attribution (Zhang 2025c). Versions as cited in paper.
gap.residue: Block-level localization inside code workflows with control flow; unaddressed: whether LLM blame is accurate, and whether localization helps beyond 3 blocks.
gap.stakes: Search cost of workflow optimization; stated qualitatively (evaluation is the dominant per-round cost).
gap.method_response: Introduce logic-block abstraction and Judge ranking so one block is edited per round.
gap.remaining_gap: Judge accuracy, comparison with textual-backprop style methods on the same blocks, larger workflows, tasks without ground-truth answers.
unresolved: Whether Judge blame beats random block choice or end-to-end signal under the same optimizer and pool.

rs_pattern.reason: Opus confirms son55. heterogeneous_decomposition requires a partition by a measured discriminating property, with a differentiated treatment per partition and a load-bearing uniform-treatment ablation. JudgeFlow's blocks are author-defined control-flow units (seq/for/cond), not partitions by a measured property. Its 'treatment' is to edit the single worst-ranked block and leave the others alone, which is a localise-and-patch move rather than a tailored per-component operation (sol itself found C04 inapplicable). decompose_and_delegate does not apply (no external solver). generative_process_redesign would need a conventionally fixed component, but the workflow was already free in AFlow; the contribution here is the attribution signal. The operation is carried by the domain cards H12/H17. The paper is fully evaluated regardless.

matches.condition_checks: S1 met (block scope); S3 partial (top-K pool, no earlier-win guard); S4 met (rank aggregation over failures); S5 partial (Judge sees traces, optimizer sees few-shot failure logs); F2 at risk (added blame signal, selection/certification unchanged from AFlow-style pool)
offline search over workflow code; F2 'incremental refinement of an existing search' applies and is only partially answered; S6 partial (held-out split + 2 transfer pairs)

pattern_mapping.operation_correspondence: Trace-level failure attribution to a workflow component followed by a scoped edit and score-gated replacement.
pattern_mapping.necessary_conditions_and_differences: Attribution is by an LLM ranking rather than code-level localization with falsifiable predictions; replacement uses a top-K pool rather than replay/regression checks; patched object is an operator-composed workflow rather than harness source.

G.reason: Both seats 2; re-checked. Coarse end-to-end signal in code-workflow search is a real limitation, and the neighbours (AFlow, MaAS, MermaidFlow, ADAS, failure attribution) are named. Not 3: TextGrad-style component-level feedback, the closest prior answer to 'where to refine', is cited only as prompt optimisation, and the residual cost of coarse signals is argued, not measured.

M.reason: Opus sides with son55. The trace → ranked blame → one-block edit → top-K chain is coherent, but its load-bearing premise is thin in ways that belong to the method, not to the evidence. (i) The Judge must emit a full ranking for every failure (opus:O01), even when no block is clearly at fault. (ii) It sees the gold answer (son55:E005). (iii) Workflows have at most 3 blocks (opus:O02), so selecting by rank-sum gains little over a random-block or whole-workflow edit, and no prediction that would separate them is stated. sol's 3 credits reconstructibility, which is X's question.

X.reason: Both seats 3; re-checked. Algorithm 1, the action set, the top-K pool and softmax parent sampling, both prompts, 20 rounds and K=3 are given. Not 4: τ, the rule that picks the reported workflow, and any regression guard or rollback are unstated.

E.measurement.reason: Both seats 3; re-checked. Standard solve-rate and pass@1 metrics are used, and the Table 1 arithmetic is internally consistent (each margin and average recomputes). Not 4: test-set sizes and contamination of public sets for gpt-4o-mini are not discussed.

E.causality.reason: Opus sides with son55. The central claim is that block-level Judge signals drive better optimisation. The only isolating comparison, the MBPP curves against AFlow, changes the representation (blocks), the signal (Judge) and the search (MCTS replaced by a top-K softmax pool, opus:O04) all at once. The Table 1 baselines follow prior literature (opus:O03) with no matched budget, and the LLM-swap table varies Judge and optimizer together. There is no Judge-off, random-block or Judge-accuracy control.

E.holdout.reason: Both seats 2; re-checked. There is a train/test split 'following previous studies' plus two zero-shot cross-benchmark pairs. Split sizes, the rule that selects the reported workflow, and per-iteration test monitoring (the MBPP test curve is plotted per iteration) are unspecified. Shared omission added: whether the MBPP 'test' operator runs public example tests or the evaluation tests is also unreported.

E.statistics.reason: Both seats 1 (A2 ladder): run counts given, no spread or test, small margins.

E.cost.reason: Both seats 1; re-checked. Only one round's GSM8K evaluation vs Judge dollars ($0.45 vs $0.01) is given. There is no total optimisation cost and no call counts against AFlow/MaAS/MermaidFlow, despite the sample-efficiency claim.
